why: The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ('erachtet ... grundsätzlich als erhebliche Beeinträchtigung') that fixing fixed or minimum resale prices is a significant restriction by object under Art. 5(1) KG, which classifies the clause beyond anything the statute itself says.

In the present tense and in its own voice ('erachtet ... grundsätzlich als erhebliche Beeinträchtigung'), the Commission classifies restrictions on the dealer's resale territory or customer group as significant under Art. 5(1) KG, which goes beyond the statute and beyond the Art. 5(4) presumption for absolute territorial protection.

The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ('erachtet ... grundsätzlich als erheblich') that restrictions on sales to end users imposed on dealers in selective distribution systems are, by their object, significant restrictions under Art. 5(1) KG, which is a classification of a clause that the statute does not itself make.

In the present tense and without citing any decision, the Commission states that it treats restrictions on cross-supplies between authorised dealers in a selective distribution system as significant restrictions under Art. 5(1) KG, which classifies a clause type in a way the statute does not.

The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ("erachtet ... grundsätzlich als erhebliche Beeinträchtigung") that restrictions preventing the supplier from selling spare parts to parties other than the dealer count as significant under Art. 5(1) KG, a classification of a clause that the statute does not itself contain.

The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ('erachtet ... grundsätzlich') that non-compete clauses exceeding five years or lasting more than one year after termination are significant restrictions under Art. 5(1) KG, a classification and duration thresholds the Cartel Act does not contain.

The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ('betrachtet ... in der Regel nicht als erheblich') a de minimis threshold of 10% market share, with an exception for cumulative effects of parallel networks, which the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that a justification "kann ... vorliegen" for more efficient distribution, and it goes beyond Art. 5(2) KG by applying this to restrictions on territory or customer groups reserved to the supplier, on the conditions that unsolicited orders may still be filled and resales by the dealer's customers are not restricted.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that territorial and customer restrictions protecting another dealer's exclusive area can be justified under Art. 5(2) KG, and it adds an example and conditions (passive sales must stay allowed and customers' resales must not be limited) that the statute does not contain.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that restrictions preventing wholesalers from selling directly to end consumers can be justified, which applies Art. 5(2) KG's efficiency grounds to a specific kind of clause that the statute does not mention.

In the present tense and in its own voice ('kann namentlich der Fall sein'), with no reference to decided cases, the Commission sets out that restrictions on selling to non-authorised dealers in a selective distribution system may be justified on efficiency grounds, an application to a kind of clause that Art. 5(2) KG does not state.

The text states in its own present-tense voice ('kann ... der Fall sein') that restrictions preventing the dealer from reselling supplied components to competing manufacturers may be justified, which adds a specific example of an efficiency justification that Art. 5(2) KG does not itself name.

The text sets out, in the present tense and without citing any decision, a criterion of its own: other vertical agreements are as a rule insignificant only below the market-share threshold of Ziffer 4(1) and absent a cumulative effect, which goes beyond the Cartel Act.

In the present tense and without citing any decision, the rule restates the Art. 5(4) KG presumption for minimum or fixed prices but adds that agreements on observing such prices that are dressed up as recommendations also count as price fixing, a classification the statute does not make.

The rule speaks in the Commission's own present-tense voice ('wird ... vermutet') without citing decided cases, and while it paraphrases the territorial-allocation presumption of Art. 5(4) KG, its parenthetical adds a criterion the statute lacks by limiting the presumption to bans on passive sales and extending it to both dealers and end customers.

The sentence states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that the presumption cannot be rebutted merely by showing interbrand competition, which is a rule on rebutting the Art. 5(4) KG presumption that the statute itself does not contain.

The sentence states in the Commission's own present-tense voice, without citing decisions, that agreements whose Art. 5(4) KG presumption is rebutted still significantly restrict competition under Art. 5(1) KG, a consequence the statute does not itself state.

The sentence states in the Commission's own present-tense voice, with no reference to decided cases, that price recommendations must be examined case by case under Art. 5 KG, which applies the statute to a kind of practice the KG does not itself mention.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, a circumstance the Commission weighs in assessing price recommendations (that they are given non-publicly, only to resellers or dealers), a criterion not found in the Cartel Act.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, a circumstance the Commission weighs in assessing price recommendations (pressure or specific incentives), a criterion the Cartel Act does not itself set out.

In the present tense and its own voice ('fallen ... ins Gewicht'), the Commission sets out a criterion for assessing price recommendations, namely that they are not expressly marked as non-binding, which the Cartel Act does not state and which is not presented as what decisions have held.

The text sets out, in present tense and without citing decisions, a circumstance the Commission weighs when assessing price recommendations (a price level clearly higher than in neighbouring countries), and this criterion is not found in the Cartel Act.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, a circumstance the Commission weighs ("fallen ... ins Gewicht") when examining price recommendations, namely actual compliance by a significant share of resellers, which is a criterion the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The notice states in its own present-tense voice, citing no decided cases, that post-term non-compete clauses longer than one year significantly restrict competition under Art. 5(1) KG and sets out three exceptions plus unlimited know-how protection, a classification and criteria the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The notice states in its own present-tense voice that agreements restricting multi-brand distribution in selective systems aimed at specific competitors' brands lead to a significant restriction of competition under Art. 5(1) KG, a classification of a clause the statute itself does not contain.

The text states in its own present-tense voice, without reference to decided cases, a reduced 5% market-share threshold for cumulative network effects and a 30% coverage criterion, neither of which the Cartel Act itself contains.

The rule says in present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that all other agreements and the exceptions in Ziffer 12 need a case-by-case check of significance, and it names selective distribution contracts that fail Ziffer 8(4) as an example, which is a classification the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The sentence sets out the assessment step in the Commission's own present-tense voice without citing decided cases, and it only paraphrases Art. 5(1) and (2) KG: an agreement that significantly restricts competition is unlawful unless economic efficiency justifies it.

The sentence states in the present tense ('gelten in der Regel ... als gerechtfertigt') a criterion the Commission applies, without reference to decided cases, and it adds to Art. 5(2) KG a 30% supplier market-share threshold for treating agreements as justified without individual assessment, together with exceptions.

The text states in the present tense, without citing any decision, that agreements outside Ziffer 15(2) get an individual assessment and are justified if they meet Art. 5(2) KG; this framing of the statutory efficiency grounds as more efficient distribution, tied to the notice's own Ziffer 15(2), goes beyond merely repeating the statute.

The rule is stated in the Commission's own present-tense voice ("können ... geltend machen") with no reference to decided cases, and it adds a specific example of an efficiency justification (time-limited protection of investments for opening new geographic or product markets) that Art. 5(2) KG itself does not list.

In the present tense and without citing any decision, the Commission names securing the uniformity and quality of the contract products as a specific example that firms may invoke under the efficiency grounds of Art. 5(2) KG, an example the statute itself does not list.

In its own present-tense voice and without citing any decision, the Commission names protection of relationship-specific investments (the hold-up problem) as an example of an Art. 5(2) KG efficiency justification, which the statute does not itself list.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that companies can invoke avoidance of free-rider-induced underinvestment in sales promotion, which is a concrete example going beyond the general efficiency grounds of Art. 5(2) KG.

The text states in its own present-tense voice that firms can invoke avoidance of double marginalisation as a justification, which is a specific example the Commission adds under the efficiency grounds of Art. 5(2) KG and which the statute itself does not name.

The item is stated in the Commission's own present-tense voice ('können ... geltend machen') with no reference to decided cases, and it goes beyond Art. 5(2) KG's general ground of disseminating technical or professional knowledge by naming, as an example for vertical agreements, the transfer of know-how qualified as 'wesentlich' (substantial).

The sentence states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that companies may invoke the securing of financial commitments not available on the capital market as a justification, which adds a specific example to the efficiency grounds of Art. 5(2) KG.

In the present tense and without citing decisions, the passage sets out the Commission's own criteria: agreements involving micro-enterprises are significant only under Art. 5(4) KG, and selective distribution means choosing dealers solely by objective qualitative product-related criteria (the excerpt appears garbled, with the second sentence truncated). The Cartel Act contains neither criterion.

The text paraphrases the Art. 5(4) KG presumption in the present tense without citing any decision, and adds a classification the statute does not make: resale price maintenance labelled as price recommendations also falls under Art. 5(4) KG.

In its own present-tense voice, the Commission states that the Art. 5(4) KG presumption cannot be rebutted by mere proof of interbrand competition, supported by legislative intent, its own assumption and EU practice rather than by its own decided cases, and this limit on how the presumption is rebutted goes beyond what the statute says.

In the present tense and without citing decided cases, the text sets out how the notice sorts agreements: some are treated as significant restrictions regardless of market share, those under Ziffer 13 are excepted, and all others need case-by-case review, none of which the Cartel Act itself says.

In its own present-tense voice, the text sets out the assessment sequence the Cartel Act already provides: a significant restriction may be justified on efficiency grounds under Art. 5(2) KG, an agreement without such grounds is unlawful, and no efficiency defence is available where effective competition is eliminated under Art. 5(4) KG; the mention of Ziffer 15 only points to where conditions are set out, and the trailing fragment about reserved customer groups looks like stray text from another provision.

The sentence states in the Commission's own present-tense voice, citing no decisions, that the Art. 5(4) KG presumption also covers agreements that lead only indirectly to minimum or fixed prices or absolute territorial protection, which the statute does not say.

The text sets out in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, how the Commission assesses significance under Art. 5(1) KG. It adds what the statute does not say: qualitative and quantitative criteria, weighed in an overall case-by-case assessment, either of which alone can make a restriction significant.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that Art. 5(4) KG agreements whose presumption is rebutted in principle meet the significance criterion of Art. 5(1) KG, a consequence the statute itself does not state.

The text states in the present tense, without citing decided cases, that Art. 5(4) KG agreements are as a rule significant regardless of market or market-share thresholds and without proof of actual effects or implementation, criteria that the Cartel Act itself does not set out.

The text states in the present tense, without citing decided cases, that certain clauses in selective distribution systems are classified as qualitatively serious and must be assessed case by case; that classification is not in the Cartel Act, even though the assessment under Art. 5(1) and 5(2) KG it then requires is statutory.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that restrictions on sales to unauthorised dealers within a selective distribution system are not qualitatively serious, and adds an example (limiting warranty services to products bought from authorised dealers) that the Cartel Act does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, citing no decided cases, that certain restrictions on sales in selective distribution count as qualitatively serious and that excluding passive sales by foreign partners generally amounts to absolute territorial protection under Art. 5(4) KG, which classifies particular clauses and applies the statute to a kind of agreement beyond what the statute itself says.

The text reads its own notice (Ziff. 12 VertBek) in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, and sets a criterion the Cartel Act does not contain: combining exclusive and selective distribution is in general qualitatively serious only when active sales are restricted, illustrated by a wholesale/retail example.

The text states criteria in the present tense without citing any decided cases: a 15% market-share safe harbour, lowered to 5% where parallel networks have cumulative effects, and a 50% coverage or top-five test for when such effects are unlikely. None of these thresholds appear in the Cartel Act.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that selective distribution systems meeting the three cumulative conditions of Ziff. 14 VertBek are permissible regardless of market shares; the Cartel Act contains no such classification or conditions.

The text uses the present tense of assessment ('gelten ... als gerechtfertigt', 'ist ... zu prüfen') with no reference to decided cases, and it adds a 30% market-share threshold, exceptions and a case-by-case efficiency review for selective distribution systems that the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that bans or restrictions on internet sales can amount to vertical price-fixing or absolute territorial protection under Art. 5(4) KG when accompanied by qualifying circumstances, and so it applies the statutory presumption to a specific kind of clause and attaches a case-by-case criterion that the statute does not contain.
The text lists, in the present tense and without reference to decided cases, examples of circumstances that qualify as a vertical price agreement, a list the Cartel Act does not contain.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, a list of example clauses (website blocking/redirection, interrupting transactions by card address) that may qualify as absolute territorial protection, examples the Cartel Act does not itself contain.

The sentence states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that bans or restrictions on internet sales count as restrictions of passive sales and are therefore qualitatively serious, a classification of a kind of clause that the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The sentence states in the present tense ('gelten ... als qualitativ schwerwiegend') and without reference to decided cases that bans or restrictions of internet sales in selective distribution systems are qualitatively serious, a classification of a clause the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The text states in the present tense ('gilt als') with no reference to decided cases that obligations imposing online-sales criteria not equivalent overall to brick-and-mortar criteria in selective distribution are qualitatively serious, and adds an equivalence criterion (same aims, comparable results, differences grounded in the nature of the channels) that the Cartel Act does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that quality requirements for internet sales (for example requiring physical points of sale, or a ban on third-party platforms in selective distribution of luxury goods) 'gelten als' not qualitatively serious, which classifies clauses beyond what the Cartel Act says.

The sentence states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that internet-sales bans or restrictions must be assessed case by case for significance and efficiency justification, which applies the Art. 5 KG assessment to a specific kind of restriction the statute does not mention.

The sentence states the sanction regime in the present tense in the Commission's own voice and cites no decided cases, but it goes beyond Art. 5(4) and Art. 49a(1) KG by extending sanctionability to Art. 5(4)-type vertical agreements that only significantly restrict competition and are not justified, which the statute does not say.

The text states in its own present-tense voice, without citing decided cases, that any form of conscious and intended cooperation qualifies and that price recommendations can amount to concerted practices given a minimal meeting of minds, which goes beyond the bare wording of Art. 4(1) and Art. 5(4) KG.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that prices can be fixed indirectly and lists examples (conditional rebates, maximum discounts, threats, delivery delays, termination), which the Cartel Act itself does not enumerate.

In its own present-tense voice and without citing decisions, the text interprets the elements of absolute territorial protection under Art. 5(4) KG: it reads 'distribution contract' broadly to cover clauses in franchise, licence and technology-transfer agreements and oral arrangements, limits the offence to excluding passive sales, and counts internet sales and tender offers as passive sales, none of which the statute says.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, which agreements count as absolute territorial protection ('Beispiele ... sind', 'gelten als'), adding examples and a classification (EEA export bans, restrictions on passive sales from selective into open distribution) that Art. 5(4) KG does not itself contain.

The text sets out in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, what counts as indirect absolute territorial protection, and it gives a list of example measures (rebate withdrawal, warranty non-reimbursement, purchase restrictions) that Art. 5(4) KG does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, a list of situations that do not on their own meet the presumption of Art. 5(4) KG (passive-sales bans binding the supplier, intra-group arrangements, pure international price differences, customer-group and internet sales restrictions, relative territorial protection), which classifies clauses and adds examples the statute does not contain.

The notice states in its own present-tense voice that territorial and customer restrictions in an exclusive distribution system are classed as qualitatively serious, with five listed exceptions such as the cap of five exclusive distributors, and Art. 5 KG contains none of this.

The Commission states in its own present-tense voice ("werden als qualitativ schwerwiegend betrachtet") that preventing effective use of the internet for sales is a qualitatively serious restriction, a classification and application to online sales that the Cartel Act does not itself contain, with no reference to decided cases.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, that companies may invoke economies of scale in distribution, a concrete example the notice adds to the general efficiency grounds of Art. 5(2) KG (such as lowering distribution costs).

The sentence states in the present tense and in the Commission's own voice, without reference to decided cases, a criterion the Cartel Act does not contain: dual pricing is in principle not a qualitatively serious vertical agreement where the wholesale price difference is proportionate to the buyer's channel-specific investments and costs.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, that wide parity obligations of online intermediation services are qualitatively serious while narrow and other parity obligations are not, a classification of clauses the Cartel Act does not contain.

The text states, in the present tense and without citing decided cases, the market-share thresholds (15 % and 30 %) and the individual-assessment rule for parity obligations, which are criteria the Cartel Act itself does not contain.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, a criterion that non-compete obligations of indefinite duration or exceeding five years are qualitatively serious, with an exception for tacit renewal and an application to indirect absolute territorial protection, none of which the Cartel Act itself says.

The text states in the present tense, without reference to decided cases, which direct means (clauses or concerted practices fixing the resale price, permitting the supplier to set it, prohibiting sales below a price level, or a buyer complying with a requested price increase) count as vertical price agreements, a list of examples that Art. 5(4) KG does not contain.

The sentence states in the present tense, without citing decided cases, a criterion the statute does not contain: maximum resale prices count as vertical price agreements when pressure or incentives make them work in fact like fixed or minimum prices.

The text sets out in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, criteria for assessing price recommendations (binding intent, concerted practice requiring contact, compliance and causality, examples such as transmission into checkout systems, effect as minimum or fixed prices through compliance, pressure or incentives), which go beyond Art. 4(1) and 5(4) KG.

The text states in the present tense, with no reference to decided cases, a list of circumstances (pressure, incentives, actual compliance, non-public communication, missing 'unverbindlich' label, price level above neighbouring countries) that may lead the Commission to take up price recommendations, criteria the Cartel Act does not itself set out.
